Centrally authorised medicinal products (EU authorisations)
The central procedure for medicinal products is utilised when authorisations are sought for the whole EEA, e.g. for biotechnological medicinal products, medicinal products for specific diseases and other innovative medicinal products. The applications are sent to the European Medicinal products Agency (EMEA). Two scientific committees, one for human medicinal products and the other for veterinary medicinal products, CHMP (Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use) and CVMP (Committee for Medicinal Products for Veterinary Use) assess the applications. Each Member State appoints one expert and one alternative for each committee. Each committee can also nominate up to five additional experts in order to cover a larger expert area. Experts from two member states from the corresponding committee are chosen for assessing each application and to write an assessment report (Rapporteur and Co-rapporteur). The other experts of the committees can comment on the assessment reports. The committees then finally issue a scientific opinion on the application. This opinion is then forwarded to the European Commission, which makes the final decision. Marketing authorisations issued by the Commission are valid in all the Member States of the EU. Other states, such as Iceland, being members of EEA but not EU, obtain additional thirty days to issue a corresponding marketing authorisation.
Nationally authorised medicinal products, mutual recognition and decentralised procedure
Applicants can choose a Member State to assess the application dossier (Reference Member State, RMS) and states where the medicinal products are intended to be placed on the market (Concerned Member States, CMS).
The Mutual Recognition Procedure
(MR) is used when a marketing authorisation has been granted for a medicine in any of the EEA states. The applicant negotiates with a state, which has granted a national marketing authorisation to write an assessment report based on the application file, i.e. to become a RMS. That assessment report is then sent along with the application dossier to the CMSs. The procedure takes 90 days if there is no dispute between the states. After the procedure has been concluded the CMSs have 30 days to review translations of texts and to issue a marketing authorisation in respective states.
The Decentralised Procedure
(DC) is most often applied when the medicine has not been nationally authorised before in any state. The application is then sent concurrently to the state responsible for the assessment report (RMS) and other CMSs. The Decentralised Procedure takes 210 days in absence of disputes. After the procedure has been concluded the CMSs have 30 days to review translations of texts and to issue a marketing authorisation in respective states.
If a CMS raises a health concern, the disagreement is referred to a specific committee, comprised of representatives from the medicinal products agencies from all the Member States, CMDh/CMDv (Coordination Group for Mutual Recognition and Decentralised Procedure human/veterinarian,
Further information
. If the dispute cannot be settled in these committees, it is referred to the scientific committees of the EMEA.

reviewed_clauses.verbatim_extracted_text:
Icelandic translations of product information texts
Before a medicinal product can be placed on the market, approved Icelandic translations of the product information texts must be available. For nationally authorised medicinal products and medicinal products approved in an MR/DC procedure, Icelandic translations of the SmPC, package leaflet and labelling shall be based on the approved English texts (common texts) and sent to the Icelandic Medicines Agency (IMA), which will assess the translations. The marketing authorisation holder is responsible for ensuring that all approved changes since the marketing authorisation was granted are included.
In addition, IMA requests the approved English product information texts (common texts) on which the Icelandic translations are based, together with a reference to the procedure number, for example: DE / H / XXXX / 001-003 / 047.
Applicants shall send the product information texts (in Word format) to IMA by email to
textar@lyfjastofnun.is
.
The subject line of the email shall be: „Íslenskir lyfjatextar fyrir [heiti lyfs] - [ferilsnúmer] vegna markaðssetningar“ (Icelandic product information texts for [name of medicinal product] - [procedure number] for marketing).
Further
information on text processing
can be found on IMA's website.
Processing time
The processing time for the assessment of Icelandic product information texts before marketing may be up to 60 days from receipt. IMA does not charge a separate fee for the assessment. Nevertheless, publication of a medicinal product in the medicines registers cannot be requested, and the medicinal product cannot be placed on the market, until the Icelandic product information texts have been approved by IMA.
Planned marketing
The applicant shall state in the email when marketing is planned. As a rule, medicinal products intended to be marketed are considered to be placed on the market within 12 months.
Medicinal products in tenders
For medicinal products that are to take part in a tender or similar, applicants shall consider that marketing of the medicinal product is planned. If it is foreseeable that the time from when the results of a tender are available until the medicinal product is to be delivered will be shorter than 60 days, the Icelandic translations must be reviewed before the tender result is available, as the processing time for the assessment of Icelandic product information texts may be up to 60 days from receipt. Fast-track processing cannot be requested for this processing time.

1. Without prejudice to Article 4(4) of Directive 2001/83/EC, a marketing authorisation which has been granted in accordance with this Regulation shall be valid throughout the Community. Centrally authorised medicinal products (EU authorisations)
The central procedure for medicinal products is utilised when authorisations are sought for the whole EEA, e.g. for biotechnological medicinal products, medicinal products for specific diseases and other innovative medicinal products. The applications are sent to the European Medicinal products Agency (EMEA). Two scientific committees, one for human medicinal products and the other for veterinary medicinal products, CHMP (Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use) and CVMP (Committee for Medicinal Products for Veterinary Use) assess the applications. Each Member State appoints one expert and one alternative for each committee. Each committee can also nominate up to five additional experts in order to cover a larger expert area. Experts from two member states from the corresponding committee are chosen for assessing each application and to write an assessment report (Rapporteur and Co-rapporteur). The other experts of the committees can comment on the assessment reports. The committees then finally issue a scientific opinion on the application. This opinion is then forwarded to the European Commission, which makes the final decision. Marketing authorisations issued by the Commission are valid in all the Member States of the EU. Other states, such as Iceland, being members of EEA but not EU, obtain additional thirty days to issue a corresponding marketing authorisation.
Nationally authorised medicinal products, mutual recognition and decentralised procedure
Applicants can choose a Member State to assess the application dossier (Reference Member State, RMS) and states where the medicinal products are intended to be placed on the market (Concerned Member States, CMS).
The Mutual Recognition Procedure
(MR) is used when a marketing authorisation has been granted for a medicine in any of the EEA states. The applicant negotiates with a state, which has granted a national marketing authorisation to write an assessment report based on the application file, i.e. to become a RMS. That assessment report is then sent along with the application dossier to the CMSs. The procedure takes 90 days if there is no dispute between the states. After the procedure has been concluded the CMSs have 30 days to review translations of texts and to issue a marketing authorisation in respective states.
The Decentralised Procedure
(DC) is most often applied when the medicine has not been nationally authorised before in any state. The application is then sent concurrently to the state responsible for the assessment report (RMS) and other CMSs. The Decentralised Procedure takes 210 days in absence of disputes. After the procedure has been concluded the CMSs have 30 days to review translations of texts and to issue a marketing authorisation in respective states.
If a CMS raises a health concern, the disagreement is referred to a specific committee, comprised of representatives from the medicinal products agencies from all the Member States, CMDh/CMDv (Coordination Group for Mutual Recognition and Decentralised Procedure human/veterinarian,
Further information
. If the dispute cannot be settled in these committees, it is referred to the scientific committees of the EMEA.

Article 13
1. Without prejudice to Article 4(4) of Directive 2001/83/EC, a marketing authorisation which has been granted in accordance with this Regulation shall be valid throughout the Community. It shall confer the same rights and obligations in each of the Member States as a marketing authorisation granted by that Member State in accordance with Article 6 of Directive 2001/83/EC.
Authorised medicinal products for human use shall be entered in the Community Register of Medicinal Products and shall be given a number, which shall appear on the packaging.
